steps.title: Import Angular modules and dependencies
steps.instruction: Import Component, OnInit, FormsModule, HttpClientModule, HttpClient, and CommonModule from their respective Angular packages.
steps.hint: Use import statements at the top of your TypeScript file. Remember to import from '@angular/core', '@angular/forms', '@angular/common/http', and '@angular/common'.
steps.seedCode: // Import the required Angular modules and dependencies here
steps.expectedOutcome: The necessary Angular modules and dependencies are imported for building a debounced search component with forms and HTTP capabilities.
successCriteria: Component, OnInit, FormsModule, HttpClientModule, HttpClient, and CommonModule are all imported from their correct Angular packages.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported all required Angular modules and dependencies. These will enable form handling, HTTP requests, and common directives for your debounced search component.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've imported some modules, but not all required ones. Check that you have Component and OnInit from '@angular/core', FormsModule from '@angular/forms', HttpClientModule and HttpClient from '@angular/common/http', and CommonModule from '@angular/common'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The imports are missing or incorrect. You need to import Component, OnInit, FormsModule, HttpClientModule, HttpClient, and CommonModule from their respective Angular packages to proceed with building the debounced search component.

steps.title: Create the main component class
steps.instruction: Create the SearchComponent class with the @Component decorator and implement the OnInit interface.
steps.hint: Use the class keyword to define the component class. Add the @Component decorator above it and implement OnInit.
steps.seedCode:
import { Component, OnInit } from '@angular/core';

// Create the SearchComponent class with @Component decorator and implement OnInit here
steps.expectedOutcome: A SearchComponent class is defined with the @Component decorator and implements OnInit.
successCriteria: SearchComponent class exists, has @Component decorator, and implements OnInit interface.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the main component class with proper Angular structure.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure your class has both the @Component decorator and implements OnInit.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component class isn't properly set up. Check that you're using @Component and implementing OnInit.

steps.title: Initialize search query state
steps.instruction: Inside the SearchComponent class, add a property named 'searchQuery' with type 'string' and initialize it as an empty string.
steps.hint: Add 'searchQuery: string = "";' inside the class body, after the constructor if present.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component now has a reactive state property to store the user's search input.
successCriteria: The SearchComponent class contains a 'searchQuery' property of type string initialized to empty string.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the searchQuery state property.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you've declared a property named 'searchQuery' with type 'string' and initialized it as empty string.
steps.feedbackWrong: The searchQuery property is missing or incorrect. It should be a string property initialized to empty string.

steps.title: Initialize search results state
steps.instruction: In the SearchComponent class, add a property named 'searchResults' with a type annotation of 'any[]' and initialize it as an empty array.
steps.hint: Add the property inside the class body, similar to how you added the searchQuery property.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a searchResults property ready to store API response data.
successCriteria: The SearchComponent class contains a 'searchResults' property typed as 'any[]' and initialized to an empty array.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added the searchResults state property to store API response data.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you've added a property named 'searchResults' with the correct type and initialization.
steps.feedbackWrong: The searchResults property is missing or incorrect. It should be typed as 'any[]' and initialized as an empty array.

steps.title: Inject HttpClient service
steps.instruction: Inject the HttpClient service in the constructor of your SearchComponent to enable HTTP requests.
steps.hint: Add a parameter with type HttpClient to the constructor and use Angular's dependency injection.
steps.analogousExample:
// Injecting a service in Angular
constructor(private http: HttpClient) {}
steps.expectedOutcome: The SearchComponent constructor now has HttpClient injected as a dependency.
successCriteria: HttpClient is properly injected in the constructor with the correct type annotation.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully injected HttpClient, which will allow your component to make API calls.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure HttpClient is properly typed in the constructor parameter.
steps.feedbackWrong: HttpClient injection is missing or incorrect. Check the constructor parameter type and import.

steps.title: Create search method
steps.instruction: Inside the SearchComponent class, create a method named performSearch that will handle the search logic. The method should be public and return void.
steps.hint: Add a method declaration inside the class body, after the constructor and ngOnInit.
steps.expectedOutcome: The SearchComponent class now contains a performSearch method declaration ready for implementing the API call logic.
successCriteria: The SearchComponent class has a public performSearch method that returns void.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the performSearch method. This method will be where we implement the HTTP request logic in the next steps.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you've created a method named performSearch that is public and returns void. Check that it's placed inside the SearchComponent class.
steps.feedbackWrong: The performSearch method is not correctly defined. Ensure you create a public method named performSearch that returns void inside the SearchComponent class.

steps.title: Add debounce timer variable
steps.instruction: Add a private property named 'debounceTimer' of type 'any' to store the setTimeout reference in your SearchComponent class.
steps.hint: Declare the property inside the class body, before the constructor. Use TypeScript's type annotation to specify the type.
steps.expectedOutcome: The SearchComponent class will have a private debounceTimer property to manage the debounce timeout.
successCriteria: The SearchComponent class contains a private property named 'debounceTimer' with type 'any'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've added the debounce timer variable. This will help manage the setTimeout reference for implementing debounced search.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you've declared a private property named 'debounceTimer' with type 'any' inside the SearchComponent class.
steps.feedbackWrong: The debounce timer variable is missing or incorrect. Add a private property named 'debounceTimer' of type 'any' to the SearchComponent class.

steps.title: Create debounced search handler
steps.instruction: Inside the SearchComponent class, create a method named onSearchInput that takes an event parameter of type Event and returns void.
steps.hint: The method signature should be onSearchInput(event: Event): void { }
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a method stub ready to implement the debounce logic in the next step.
successCriteria: The SearchComponent class contains an onSearchInput method with the signature (event: Event): void
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created the handler method. Next we'll add the debounce logic inside it.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure the method is named exactly 'onSearchInput' and takes an Event parameter.
steps.feedbackWrong: The method is missing or has incorrect signature. It should be onSearchInput(event: Event): void.

steps.title: Add template structure with search input
steps.instruction: In the component decorator's template property, add an input element with two-way binding to the searchQuery property using [(ngModel)].
steps.hint: Use the Angular template syntax with ngModel for two-way data binding between the input field and the searchQuery property.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component template now contains an input element that will update the searchQuery property when the user types.
successCriteria: The template property contains an input element with [(ngModel)] binding to searchQuery.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added the search input with two-way binding to the searchQuery property.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added an input element, but it needs two-way binding using [(ngModel)] to connect with searchQuery.
steps.feedbackWrong: The template still doesn't have the required input element with two-way binding to searchQuery.

steps.title: Wire input event to debounced handler
steps.instruction: In the component's template, add an (input) event binding to the search input element that calls the onSearchInput method with $event.target.value.
steps.hint: Use Angular's event binding syntax: (input)="onSearchInput($event.target.value)" on the input element.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: binding input event to a handler
<input (input)="handleInput($event.target.value)" />
steps.expectedOutcome: The search input element will have an event binding that triggers the onSearchInput method whenever the user types.
successCriteria: The input element in the template includes (input)="onSearchInput($event.target.value)" binding.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully wired the input event to your debounced handler. Now when users type, the onSearchInput method will be called with the current input value.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using Angular's event binding syntax correctly. The input element should have (input)="onSearchInput($event.target.value)".
steps.feedbackWrong: The input event isn't properly connected to the handler. Remember to use Angular's (input) event binding and pass $event.target.value to the onSearchInput method.

steps.title: Add results display section
steps.instruction: Add a <div> element below the search input to display the search results. Use *ngFor to iterate over the searchResults array and show each result item.
steps.hint: Use Angular's *ngFor directive to loop through the searchResults array and display each item. You can use interpolation {{ }} to show the result value.
steps.analogousExample:
// Displaying list items with *ngFor
  • {{ item.name }}
steps.expectedOutcome: The template will have a results section that displays each item from the searchResults array.
successCriteria: A <div> element with *ngFor directive is added to the template, iterating over searchResults and displaying each item.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added the results display section. The search results will now be shown when available.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using *ngFor correctly to iterate over searchResults and display each item.
steps.feedbackWrong: The results display section wasn't added correctly. Check that you're using *ngFor to loop through searchResults and display each result.

steps.title: Add loading state and cleanup
steps.instruction: Add a loading state property to track when searches are in progress and implement the ngOnDestroy lifecycle hook to clear the debounce timer.
steps.hint: Add a boolean property called 'isLoading' initialized to false, then implement the ngOnDestroy method to clear the debounceTimer if it exists.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a loading state property and proper cleanup of the debounce timer when the component is destroyed.
successCriteria: Component has 'isLoading' boolean property initialized to false and implements ngOnDestroy method that clears debounceTimer
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added loading state tracking and implemented proper cleanup for the debounce timer.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've added both the isLoading property and the ngOnDestroy method with timer cleanup.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component still needs a loading state property and lifecycle cleanup. Review the Angular lifecycle hooks and timer management.
